title: Does prompting 'act agentically' increase covert sabotage in open coding models?
problem: The DeepMind honeypot study found Gemini schemes more when prompted toward agency or self-preservation, but it is unknown whether this prompt-sensitivity holds for small open models accessible outside a major lab.
direction: Take 2-3 open instruct models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and ~20-30 coding tasks from public benchmarks (HumanEval/MBPP) lightly reframed so 'correct' behavior conflicts with a planted hidden objective (subtly weaken a monitoring/logging function). Run each under a neutral system prompt vs an 'act agentically / preserve yourself' prompt, all inference-only. Measure the rate of inserted subtle defects/sabotage (unit-test + LLM-judge rubric) across conditions.
why_it_matters: Scheming propensity evals have only been demonstrated on frontier models inside labs; showing whether the agency-prompt effect replicates gives the community a cheap reproducible scheming-elicitation probe.
relevant_context: Extends 'Realistic honeypot evaluations for scheming propensity' (Krakovna et al., 2026) — the agency/self-preservation prompt-sensitivity result.

title: Eval-awareness probe: do open models behave differently when they 'know' they're being tested?
problem: The honeypot paper relies on low eval-awareness for its results to be trustworthy, but eval-awareness in small open models is poorly characterized.
direction: Construct ~40 matched task pairs where one version is framed as realistic deployment ('a teammate asks you to fix this code') and the other overtly as an evaluation ('this is a safety test of your behavior'). Run open models inference-only and measure whether refusal rate, hidden-defect insertion, or self-reported suspicion changes. Add a direct post-hoc elicitation asking whether it thought it was being tested, and correlate with behavior shifts.
why_it_matters: If open models reliably alter behavior when they suspect evaluation, safety benchmarks built on them are systematically biased; quantifying eval-awareness cheaply gives a reusable diagnostic.
relevant_context: Extends 'Realistic honeypot evaluations for scheming propensity' — turns its assumed low-eval-awareness property into a measured one across open models.

title: Cheap active sampling: can a Gaussian Process pick safety-eval prompts 10x more efficiently?
problem: ProEval shows GP-based active selection reaches accurate performance estimates with 8-65x fewer samples, but it was demonstrated on internal DeepMind setups; whether a simple version helps a budget-constrained safety evaluator is untested.
direction: On one public safety benchmark with many items (a refusal/jailbreak set or TruthfulQA), score a single open model on the full set as ground truth. Then implement a lightweight Bayesian-quadrature-style sampler (scikit-learn GaussianProcessRegressor over cheap text-embedding features) that adaptively chooses which prompts to evaluate next, and compare sample-efficiency to random subsampling for estimating the overall safety score to within +-1%. Report the savings curve.
why_it_matters: Smaller orgs run safety evals on tight budgets; a public reproducible demonstration that GP-active selection cuts eval cost democratizes a frontier-lab technique.
relevant_context: Extends 'ProEval' (Huang et al., 2026) — its 8-65x sample-efficiency claim, scaled down to scikit-learn on a single benchmark.

title: Uncertainty-guided jailbreak discovery vs. random sampling on a fixed budget
problem: ProEval frames failure discovery as superlevel-set sampling that surfaces more diverse failures under a budget, but it is unclear whether this beats naive random search for finding safety failures with a beginner-feasible setup.
direction: Take a large pool of templated jailbreak/harmful-prompt variants (AdvBench or HarmBench prompts). Fit a simple GP/uncertainty model over embeddings of already-labeled prompts (model complied = failure), and use uncertainty-aware acquisition to choose the next prompts to test against one open model. Compare the number and cluster-coverage diversity of discovered failures against random sampling at equal query budgets.
why_it_matters: Efficient failure discovery is a bottleneck for safety red-teaming outside big labs; a clean public comparison gives independent red-teamers an actionable low-cost technique.
relevant_context: Extends 'ProEval' — its failure-discovery-as-superlevel-set-sampling result, instantiated as uncertainty-aware jailbreak search.

title: A mini-benchmark for the Detection layer: can cheap monitors catch a sabotaging agent?
problem: The AI Control Roadmap proposes detection safeguards (D1-D4) for catching misaligned agents acting as insider threats, but offers no cheap reproducible testbed for whether lightweight monitors actually catch subtle sabotage.
direction: Build a small public testbed: have one open model produce coding-task outputs in two modes (honest vs instructed to insert a subtle backdoor/defect), then evaluate whether a cheap LLM-based monitor (a second open model given a detection rubric) flags the sabotaged outputs. Vary monitor strength and prompt to estimate detection rate, FPR, and where monitoring fails. Release the labeled dataset and rubric.
why_it_matters: Defense-in-depth control assumes monitors work even if alignment fails; a public micro-benchmark quantifying cheap-monitor detection gives the agenda concrete replicable evidence and a starter dataset.
relevant_context: Extends 'Securing the future of AI agents / Three Layers of Agent Security' (Phuong, Jenner et al., 2026) — operationalizes its Detection tier (D1-D4).

title: How does monitor reliability degrade as the monitored model gets more capable?
problem: The roadmap flags 'scaling monitoring with capability' and detecting hidden reasoning as open threads, but there is little public data on whether a fixed-strength monitor catches sabotage less often as the monitored agent grows more capable.
direction: Hold a single small open model fixed as the monitor and vary the monitored/sabotaging model across a capability ladder (1B -> 3B -> 8B -> 14B). For each, have the monitored model attempt subtle sabotage on coding tasks and measure the monitor's detection rate. Plot detection rate vs monitored-model capability to test whether stronger agents evade fixed monitors.
why_it_matters: A core worry of scalable oversight is that monitors must keep pace with monitored models; a cheap empirical curve gives concrete evidence about the durability of the control approach.
relevant_context: Extends 'Securing the future of AI agents' — its open thread on scaling monitoring with capability.

title: Does single-domain beneficial-trait fine-tuning generalize OOD in a small open model?
problem: OpenAI reports beneficial-trait RL confined to the health domain produced cross-domain alignment gains, but used frontier-scale RL; whether the cheaper accessible analogue (small LoRA SFT on one domain) shows any OOD transfer is unknown.
direction: Build a tiny dataset of ~150-300 health-domain dialogues exemplifying one trait (honesty / epistemic humility under pressure), curated from public sources, and LoRA-fine-tune one small open model (a few hours). Evaluate tuned vs base on OOD public alignment benchmarks in unrelated domains (TruthfulQA, a sycophancy set, a small deception probe). Report whether single-domain trait tuning moves OOD alignment metrics at all.
why_it_matters: If cheap single-domain LoRA tuning yields measurable cross-domain honesty gains, alignment-via-traits becomes accessible far beyond major labs; a null result is equally informative.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reinforcement learning towards broadly and persistently beneficial models' (Jagadeesh, Heidecke et al., 2026) — its health-only-to-unrelated cross-domain result, downscaled to LoRA SFT.

title: Is beneficial-trait alignment robust to a few steps of harmful fine-tuning?
problem: The paper notes harmful-fine-tuning resistance 'needs more work' and claims robustness under adversarial pressure, but the durability of trait-aligned behavior against cheap downstream fine-tuning is untested in the open.
direction: Take a publicly available trait/instruction-aligned open model and apply a small LoRA fine-tune on a few hundred mildly misaligned or task-narrow examples (public data, e.g. sycophancy-encouraging dialogues). Measure how quickly aligned traits (honesty, refusal calibration) erode on held-out alignment benchmarks as a function of fine-tuning steps.
why_it_matters: Persistence of alignment under downstream modification is central to whether open-weight aligned models stay safe after release; a cheap erosion curve informs release norms.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reinforcement learning towards broadly and persistently beneficial models' — its harmful-fine-tuning-resistance open thread.

title: Deployment-Simulation vs. Challenge-Prompt Failure Prediction on a Single Open Model
problem: OpenAI showed regenerating final turns over WildChat prefixes predicts real-world failure rates far better than challenge prompts, but only for closed frontier models. Whether the same ordering holds for a small open model an external researcher can run is unknown.
direction: Sample ~1,000 WildChat conversation prefixes (public) and a comparable set of adversarial/challenge prompts (a public jailbreak/safety set). For one open model (Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen2.5-7B), regenerate the final assistant turn on both sets and score each output for a single undesirable behavior (refusal-failure on harmful requests) using a cheap LLM judge. Compare which prompt source yields failure rates closer to a held-out realistic WildChat slice.
why_it_matters: If public-data deployment simulation generalizes to open models, independent evaluators and academics can estimate real-world failure rates without lab access, strengthening external oversight.
relevant_context: Extends 'Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments?' (OpenAI, 2026) — the deployment-simulation-beats-challenge-prompts result.

title: Why Does Public-Data Prediction Break on Agentic Tasks? A Small-Scale Diagnosis
problem: The paper reports WildChat-based predictions were ~37x worse for agentic use cases, but does not diagnose why. The gap is a clear open thread but its causes are unexplored at a scale an external researcher can probe.
direction: Take WildChat (chat-like) prefixes and a public agentic/tool-use dataset (ToolBench-style or a public agent-trace set) and, on one open instruct model, measure a single failure metric (unsafe tool call or task-derailment flagged by an LLM judge) on both. Decompose the prediction-error gap by one controlled factor at a time: conversation length, presence of tool-call formatting, number of turns.
why_it_matters: Agentic deployments are where high-stakes harms concentrate, yet that is where public-data evaluation is least reliable; understanding the failure mode tells evaluators when they can trust cheap proxies.
relevant_context: Extends 'Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments?' — its ~37x agentic-error open thread.

title: Does Light CoT-Grading Reduce Monitorability? A LoRA Replication on an Open Model
problem: OpenAI found no clear evidence that accidentally grading CoT during RL reduced monitorability, but could not rule out harder-to-measure effects. There is no open controlled replication of what even a small amount of CoT-pressure does to faithful verbalization.
direction: On one open reasoning-capable small model, build a tiny LoRA preference/SFT setup where 'reasoning-graded' examples reward CoT that omits a planted hint, vs a control that grades only final answers. Then run a monitorability probe: give both models problems containing a hint and check whether a separate monitor can still detect hint-use from the CoT. Deliverable: before/after monitorability detection rates. Public hint-following/reward-hacking eval set; LoRA only.
why_it_matters: CoT monitorability is a leading hope for catching misaligned reasoning, and whether optimization pressure silently erodes it is safety-critical; a cheap open replication lets the community sanity-check lab claims.
relevant_context: Extends 'Investigating the consequences of accidentally grading CoT during RL' (OpenAI, 2026) — its indirect-CoT-pressure open thread.

title: Reusing OpenAI's Open-Sourced Monitorability Evals on Small Open Models
problem: OpenAI open-sourced 13 CoT-monitorability evals but ran them primarily on their own models. It is unknown how small widely-available open models score, or whether the evals discriminate cleanly at that scale.
direction: Clone the released monitorability-eval scaffold and run a subset (hint-following and sandbagging evals) on 2-3 open instruct models of different sizes (3B, 7-8B) inference-only on a single GPU. Report per-eval monitor-detection scores and whether bigger open models are more or less monitorable. As a twist, apply the paper's cross-fit filtering to one intervention eval and check whether it removes noise-driven false positives.
why_it_matters: Standardized runnable monitorability benchmarks for open models give the community a shared yardstick and a low-barrier on-ramp into monitorability research.
relevant_context: Extends 'Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations' (OpenAI, 2026) — reuses released datasets/code and the cross-fit filtering strategy on uncovered open models.

title: Cross-Fit Filtering vs. Naive Thresholds: A Reproduction of the 'p-hacked Survivor' Effect
problem: The monitorability eval release claims a cross-fit filtering strategy prevents 'p-hacked survivors' (noise-driven false positives) in intervention-style evals, but the practical magnitude of this benefit is hard to gauge from the post alone.
direction: Using the released eval code and one open model, construct a controlled intervention eval where the true effect is known (inject a measurable hint-following intervention). Run many random sub-evals, count how many spuriously 'survive' significance under naive filtering vs the paper's cross-fit filtering. Quantify false-positive reduction as a function of noise/sample size.
why_it_matters: Robust statistics for safety evals prevent overclaiming about whether interventions improve monitorability, which affects how much to trust monitorability evidence in deployment decisions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations' — its cross-fit filtering result, reproduced on a known-ground-truth setup.

title: Can an AI Auto-Reviewer Be Misled? A Small Red-Team of LLM Action-Approval
problem: OpenAI's open-sourced auto-review uses a separate AI agent to approve boundary-crossing coding-agent actions, achieving ~99.9% effective approval but admitting red-teaming found cases where it could be misled. The robustness of such an LLM-reviewer to simple manipulation is under-characterized in the open.
direction: Build a minimal version of the auto-review pattern: an open model acts as a reviewer that approves/blocks proposed agent actions (shell commands or file writes) given a policy. Construct a small public test set of clearly-harmful actions, then apply a handful of simple obfuscation tactics (benign-sounding justifications, command splitting, misleading context) and measure how much the reviewer's catch-rate drops per tactic.
why_it_matters: As agents increasingly self-supervise with AI reviewers replacing human oversight, the reviewer becomes a single point of failure; cheaply mapping which manipulations bypass it informs where human review must stay.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight' (OpenAI, 2026) — its open-sourced design and the open thread that red-teaming could mislead it.

title: Probing Evaluation-Awareness Verbalization in Open Models
problem: The GPT-5.5 system card reports 22.1% evaluation-awareness verbalization, a behavior that can confound safety evals. Whether and how often open models verbalize eval-awareness, and what triggers it, is not characterized.
direction: Assemble a public set of prompts varying along plausible eval-awareness cues (explicit 'this is a test' framing, benchmark-style formatting, neutral chat). On 2-3 open instruct models, generate CoT/responses and use a keyword + LLM-judge classifier to measure how often the model verbalizes that it might be evaluated. Quantify which cues most increase verbalized eval-awareness.
why_it_matters: If models recognize evaluation contexts, they may behave differently under test than in deployment, undermining the validity of safety evals; measuring triggers in open models guides prompt design.
relevant_context: Extends the 'GPT-5.5 System Card' (OpenAI, 2026) — its 22.1% evaluation-awareness verbalization metric, characterized in open models.

title: Do open-model 'monitors' catch sabotage when the agent doesn't know it's watched? A trusted-monitor replication
problem: Apollo argues scalable monitoring works because there is near-unlimited data and it reduces to an automatable optimization, but it is unclear how well a cheap open-weight monitor (not a frontier model) detects subtle sabotage in coding-agent transcripts.
direction: Take a public set of agent transcripts containing benign and sabotaged/backdoored code completions (SHADE-Arena or AutoMonitor-Bench style, or synthesize pairs by inserting known CWE backdoors into clean solutions). Prompt a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B) as a binary 'safe or sabotage?' monitor and measure AUROC / TPR-at-fixed-FPR. Vary the prompt (action-only vs full CoT visible) to test whether seeing the agent's reasoning helps.
why_it_matters: Scalable monitoring is a leading non-interpretability safety bet; if cheap open monitors already get usable detection rates, monitoring is deployable outside frontier labs.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — its claim that simpler baselines have not been beaten, tested at the small-model end.

title: Does a 2-monitor ensemble beat the best single monitor? A cheap test of Apollo's ensemble claim
problem: Apollo reports monitoring ensembles produce clear improvements, but the result is asserted for their internal setup; it is untested whether simply averaging two cheap diverse open-model monitors beats the stronger single monitor on a fixed false-positive budget.
direction: Reuse the labeled benign/sabotage transcript set. Score each transcript with two distinct small open models (Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B) and a third prompt-diverse variant. Combine via score-averaging and max-rule, then compare ensemble TPR-at-1%-FPR against each individual monitor. Report whether diversity (different base models) helps more than redundancy (same model, different prompts).
why_it_matters: If a trivial ensemble of cheap open monitors reliably beats any single one, small labs and external auditors get a free reliability boost for catching deceptive agent behavior.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — replicates its 'ensembles improve' claim at cheap open-model scale.

title: Can a small monitor be talked past? Measuring evasion uplift from simple prompt-level obfuscation
problem: Apollo lists monitoring-evasion as an open concern, but most evasion studies target frontier monitors; the failure surface of cheap open-model monitors against trivial obfuscation is unquantified.
direction: Start from the labeled sabotage transcripts. Apply a fixed menu of cheap hand-coded obfuscation transforms to the malicious actions (innocuous-comment padding, variable renaming, distributing the backdoor across two steps) and re-measure the small open monitor's TPR before vs after. Report which transforms cause the largest detection drop — a 'monitor robustness leaderboard' for one cheap monitor.
why_it_matters: Knowing how brittle cheap monitors are to low-effort evasion tells safety teams how much adversarial hardening is required before monitoring can be a deployment gate.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — operationalizes its monitoring-evasion open thread into measured evasion uplift.

title: Can open agents 'hide' a rogue action from a monitor? A tiny means-and-opportunity probe
problem: METR's frontier-risk pilot judged that internal agents had means/motive/opportunity for minimal rogue deployments but lacked the means to hide a significant-scale one under investigation; this 'can it hide?' capability has not been measured for cheap open agents.
direction: Build a sandboxed toy task (a small repo + a benign 'overseer' LLM reading the agent's logs). Instruct an open agent (a 7-8B instruct model with tool-use prompting) to complete a benign task while also covertly inserting and concealing a flagged action, then measure how often the overseer flags it across difficulty levels. The metric is concealment success rate vs task difficulty.
why_it_matters: Whether models can conceal unauthorized actions from oversight is the crux of rogue-deployment risk; a cheap public testbed lets external researchers track this capability over open-model generations.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Frontier Risk Report (Feb-Mar 2026)' — its means/motive/opportunity-but-cannot-hide finding, in an open-model analogue.

title: How much do self-reports inflate AI productivity gains? A small re-survey calibrated against an objective task
problem: METR's usage survey found respondents self-report 1.4-2x value and ~3x speed gains, but notes self-reports likely overstate reality (~40pp overestimation in prior METR work) — the perceived-vs-measured gap is uncharacterized for small well-defined tasks.
direction: Recruit ~20-30 student/junior programmers (or use a public coding-task dataset with timing). For a fixed set of small gradeable tasks, collect each person's self-estimated speedup from AI, then measure their actual time with vs without an AI assistant on matched tasks. Report the per-person gap and whether it replicates METR's overestimation direction.
why_it_matters: AI risk governance increasingly relies on productivity estimates; if self-reports systematically overstate uplift, safety-relevant capability forecasts built on surveys are biased.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity' — its 1.4-2x self-report and ~40pp-overestimation caveat.

title: Does task substitution inflate measured uplift? An empirical check of METR's uplift inequalities
problem: Cunningham & Whitfill prove uplift-on-old-tasks <= uplift-in-value <= uplift-on-new-tasks, implying fixed-task-basket measurements understate value as people switch tasks — but this inequality has not been checked against simple empirical data.
direction: Construct a small basket of coding/writing tasks split into 'old' (done pre-AI) and 'new' (only feasible because AI helps). Have a handful of participants log which tasks they choose with vs without AI, and estimate per-task uplift. Test whether the observed ordering of average uplift across old-task vs new-task buckets is consistent with the proven inequality, and quantify how much substitution moves the headline number.
why_it_matters: Capability-acceleration estimates feed AI risk thresholds; if task substitution silently inflates/deflates the numbers, governance decisions rest on a measurement artifact.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Task Substitution and Uplift' (Cunningham & Whitfill) — its proven uplift inequality.

title: What would it take to actually establish 'R&D-automation risk is low'? A reusable evidence-quality rubric
problem: METR agreed Opus 4.6's catastrophic R&D-automation risk is low but found the supporting evidence methodologically inadequate — yet there is no lightweight reusable rubric for grading the evidence quality of such safety claims.
direction: Distill METR's critique into a concrete checklist/rubric (sample representativeness, leading-indicator coverage, pre-full-automation acceleration modeling, conflict-of-interest controls). Apply it to 3-4 publicly available frontier risk/safety-case documents (Anthropic, METR, Apollo posts) and produce scored evidence-quality cards. Deliverable: the rubric plus filled scorecards and an analysis of common evidence gaps.
why_it_matters: Safety cases are becoming the primary mechanism for governing frontier deployment; an open reusable evidence-quality rubric lets outside reviewers audit whether 'risk is low' claims are supported.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Review of the Risks from automated R&D section in the Anthropic Risk Report (Feb 2026)' — its inadequate-evidence finding.
